questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A patent owner sues a competitor for infringement and obtains a restraining order. In its own complaint, the patent owner admits that its patent is valid only until a certain date. By the time an appellate court approves the bond and issues a restraining order against the competitor, that date has passed. Was the restraining order proper? Explain, based on Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The patent owner's exclusive right exists only during the term of the patent. After the patent expired, there was no right left to protect, so no restraining order or injunction could properly issue.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 37 of Republic Act No. 165, the exclusive right of the patentee to make, use and sell the patented article exists throughout the Philippines for the term of the patent, and the term was seventeen years from the date of issuance (Section 21). Under Section 4, Rule 129 of the Rules of Court, an admission made by a party in the same case does not require proof and may be contradicted only by showing palpable mistake or that no such admission was made. Two requisites must exist for injunctive relief: (1) a clear and unmistakable right that must be protected; and (2) an urgent and paramount necessity for the writ to prevent serious damage.
suggestedAnswer.application: The patent owner admitted in its complaint the dates of issuance and of expiry, so the expiry needs no further evidence, and there is no showing of palpable mistake. After that date it no longer had the exclusive right to make, use and sell the patented articles. When the appellate court issued the restraining order, the first requisite, a clear right to be protected, was missing. Since the patent that was the basis of the injunction was no longer valid, the question of extending an injunction became moot and academic, and the case should have been dismissed.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The restraining order was improper, and the petition that sought to extend the injunction should have been dismissed as moot and academic.

keyPoints: The patentee's exclusive right to make, use and sell exists only during the term of the patent (Section 37, R.A. No. 165; seventeen years under Section 21)
An admission in the same case needs no proof unless made through palpable mistake or never made (Section 4, Rule 129)
Injunctive relief needs a clear and unmistakable right to be protected and an urgent and paramount necessity to prevent serious damage
After the patent expired there was no right to protect, so the restraining order was improper
The issue of extending the injunction was moot and academic once the patent was no longer valid

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the first issue (injunction after the patent has lapsed)
source.excerpt: It is clear from the above-quoted provision of law that the exclusive right of a patentee to make, use and sell a patented product, article or process exists only during the term of the patent. … On the basis of the foregoing, the Court agrees with petitioner that after July 16, 2004, respondents no longer possess the exclusive right to make, use and sell the articles or products covered by Philippine Letters Patent No. 21116. … From the foregoing, it can be inferred that two requisites must exist to warrant the issuance of an injunctive relief, namely: (1) the existence of a clear and unmistakable right that must be protected; and (2) an urgent and paramount necessity for the writ to prevent serious damage. In the instant case, it is clear that when the CA issued its January 18, 2005 Resolution approving the bond filed by respondents, the latter no longer had a right that must be protected, considering that Philippine Letters Patent No. 21116 which was issued to them already expired on July 16, 2004. Hence, the issuance by the CA of a temporary restraining order in favor of the respondents is not proper.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company sues a competitor for patent infringement before an intellectual property agency, asking for damages and a permanent injunction. While that case is pending, the company files a second action against the same competitor in a regional trial court on the basis of a different patent for the same product, asking for the same kind of injunction and damages. The company argues that there can be no forum shopping because the two complaints rely on different patents. Is it right? What should happen to the second case? Explain, based on Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The company is guilty of forum shopping. A difference in the patents does not change the cause of action, because the rights violated, the acts complained of and the reliefs sought are the same. The second case should be dismissed.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: A cause of action is the act or omission by which a party violates a right of another (Section 2, Rule 2). Forum shopping exists where there is identity of parties, identity of the rights asserted and reliefs prayed for, founded on the same facts, and identity such that a judgment in one action would amount to res judicata in the other. What matters is the vexation caused to courts and litigants by a party who asks different courts or agencies to rule on the same or related causes or to grant substantially the same reliefs, creating a possibility of conflicting decisions. If forum shopping is not willful and deliberate, the subsequent case is dismissed without prejudice on the ground of litis pendentia or res judicata; if it is willful and deliberate, all the actions are dismissed with prejudice.
suggestedAnswer.application: In both complaints the company claimed an exclusive right to make, use and sell the same product and said the competitor violated it by importing, distributing and selling it. It asked for substantially the same restraining order, injunction, damages and forfeiture. That the patents were different is immaterial. A decision in one case would necessarily amount to res judicata in the other. If the company did not act willfully and deliberately, for example because it could believe that different patents allowed separate actions and it candidly told the second court of the pending case, then only the later case is dismissed, without prejudice, on the ground of litis pendentia.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The company committed forum shopping, and the second case should be dismissed on the ground of litis pendentia, without prejudice, unless the forum shopping was willful and deliberate, in which case both would be dismissed with prejudice.

keyPoints: A cause of action is the act or omission by which a party violates a right of another
The patents being different is immaterial if the rights violated, the acts and the reliefs are identical
Filing two apparently different actions with the same objective is forum shopping
A decision in one case would be res judicata in the other
If not willful and deliberate, the later case is dismissed without prejudice on litis pendentia or res judicata; if willful and deliberate, all actions are dismissed with prejudice

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the third issue (forum shopping)
source.excerpt: Section 2, Rule 2 of the Rules of Court defines a cause of action as the act or omission by which a party violates a right of another. … Thus, it does not matter that the patents upon which the complaints were based are different. The fact remains that in both complaints the rights violated and the acts violative of such rights are identical. … Owing to the substantial identity of parties, reliefs and issues in the IPO and RTC cases, a decision in one case will necessarily amount to res judicata in the other action. It bears to reiterate that what is truly important to consider in determining whether forum shopping exists or not is the vexation caused the courts and parties-litigant by a party who asks different courts and/or administrative agencies to rule on the same or related causes and/or to grant the same or substantially the same reliefs, in the process creating the possibility of conflicting decisions being rendered by the different fora upon the same issue.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: The Bureau of Legal Affairs of the Intellectual Property Office issues a preliminary injunction in a patent infringement complaint but refuses to extend it. The patent owner challenges the refusal by a special civil action for certiorari in the Court of Appeals. The adverse party says that, under the Intellectual Property Code, only the Director General of the Intellectual Property Office can review the Bureau's rulings. Which tribunal has jurisdiction? Explain, based on Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The Court of Appeals has jurisdiction. The Director General reviews decisions of the Bureau, but the patent owner is challenging an interlocutory order, and for that there is no remedy within the agency, so certiorari under the Rules of Court in the Court of Appeals is proper.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Section 7(b) of Republic Act No. 8293, the Director General exercises exclusive appellate jurisdiction over decisions of the Director of the Bureau of Legal Affairs. But the Code is silent about any remedy against interlocutory orders of the Bureau, and the rules on administrative complaints for violations of intellectual property laws provide that interlocutory orders are not appealable. Where no remedy is prescribed within the administrative machinery, the Rules of Court apply suppletorily, so a special civil action for certiorari under Rule 65 is available when a party cannot appeal and has no other plain, speedy and adequate remedy. The doctrine of primary jurisdiction does not apply when the question is purely legal and will ultimately have to be decided by the courts.
suggestedAnswer.application: What the patent owner questions is not a decision but an interlocutory order denying the extension of a preliminary injunction. It cannot appeal that order and has no other plain, speedy and adequate remedy. Whether to extend the injunction is a purely legal question that does not need the agency's special knowledge of technical matters, and courts have the duty to determine whether there was grave abuse of discretion on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the government. The patent owner therefore correctly went to the Court of Appeals.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The Court of Appeals, not the Director General, has jurisdiction to review the Bureau's interlocutory order by certiorari.

keyPoints: Section 7(b) of R.A. No. 8293: the Director General has exclusive appellate jurisdiction over decisions of the Director of the Bureau of Legal Affairs
The Code is silent on remedies against interlocutory orders, and the IPO's rules say interlocutory orders are not appealable
In the absence of an agency remedy, the Rules of Court apply suppletorily, so certiorari under Rule 65 in the Court of Appeals is proper
An exception to primary jurisdiction is a purely legal question that will ultimately be decided by the courts
Courts decide whether any branch or instrumentality of government committed grave abuse of discretion

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the second issue (which tribunal reviews interlocutory orders of the BLA-IPO)
source.excerpt: It is true that under Section 7(b) of RA 8293, otherwise known as the Intellectual Property Code of the Philippines, which is the presently prevailing law, the Director General of the IPO exercises exclusive appellate jurisdiction over all decisions rendered by the Director of the BLA-IPO. However, what is being questioned before the CA is not a decision, but an interlocutory order of the BLA-IPO denying respondents' motion to extend the life of the preliminary injunction issued in their favor. RA 8293 is silent with respect to any remedy available to litigants who intend to question an interlocutory order issued by the BLA-IPO. Moreover, Section 1(c), Rule 14 of the Rules and Regulations on Administrative Complaints for Violation of Laws Involving Intellectual Property Rights simply provides that interlocutory orders shall not be appealable. … Hence, in the absence of such a remedy, the provisions of the Rules of Court shall apply in a suppletory manner, as provided under Section 3, Rule 1 of the same Rules and Regulations. Hence, in the present case, respondents correctly resorted to the filing of a special civil action for certiorari with the CA to question the assailed Orders of the BLA-IPO, as they cannot appeal therefrom and they have no other plain, speedy and adequate remedy in the ordinary course of law.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In its complaint, a patent owner states the date its patent was issued and the date until which the patent is valid. Later, in the same case, the other party asks the court to require proof that the patent has expired on that date. According to Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc., how should the court treat the patent owner's statement?

choices.A: It is an admission that needs no proof and may be contradicted only by showing palpable mistake or that no such admission was made.
choices.B: It is only a claim and must be proved by evidence like any other fact.
choices.C: It binds only the patent owner in a different case, not in the same case.
choices.D: It can be freely withdrawn at any time before judgment.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Court noted that the patent owners themselves admitted in their complaint the date of issuance and that the patent was valid until July 16, 2004, which accords with Section 21 of Republic Act No. 165 (a term of seventeen years from issuance). Under Section 4, Rule 129 of the Rules of Court, an admission made by a party in the course of the proceedings in the same case does not require proof, and it may be contradicted only by showing that it was made through palpable mistake or that no such admission was made. There was no such showing, so there was no need to present evidence of the expiry. B is wrong because admissions in the same case need no proof. C is wrong because the rule covers admissions in the same case. D is wrong because an admission can be contradicted only on the grounds stated.

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the first issue (the term of the patent and the admission)
source.excerpt: They also admitted that the validity of the said patent is until July 16, 2004, which is in conformity with Section 21 of RA 165, providing that the term of a patent shall be seventeen (17) years from the date of issuance thereof. Section 4, Rule 129 of the Rules of Court provides that an admission, verbal or written, made by a party in the course of the proceedings in the same case, does not require proof and that the admission may be contradicted only by showing that it was made through palpable mistake or that no such admission was made.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: According to Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc., which of the following correctly states the elements of forum shopping?

choices.A: Only that the same party filed two cases in the same year.
choices.B: Only that both cases involve the same patent.
choices.C: (a) Identity of parties, or of parties representing the same interests; (b) identity of the rights asserted and reliefs prayed for, founded on the same facts; and (c) identity of the two preceding particulars such that a judgment in one action would amount to res judicata in the other.
choices.D: Only that a party lost in one forum and then filed an appeal in a higher court.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The decision lists these three elements. A and B state only one fact and are not the test; in this very case the two complaints relied on different patents, and the Court still found forum shopping because the rights violated, the acts and the reliefs were identical. D is wrong because forum shopping excludes seeking review by appeal or by the special civil action of certiorari; it is the seeking of another opinion in another forum, or the filing of two or more actions grounded on the same cause on the supposition that one or the other court would make a favorable disposition.

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the third issue (the elements of forum shopping)
source.excerpt: The elements of forum shopping are: (a) identity of parties, or at least such parties that represent the same interests in both actions; (b) identity of rights asserted and reliefs prayed for, the reliefs being founded on the same facts; (c) identity of the two preceding particulars, such that any judgment rendered in the other action will, regardless of which party is successful, amount to res judicata in the action under consideration.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A court of appeals is asked to review a refusal to extend a preliminary injunction that was issued to protect a patent. While the appeal is pending, the patent lapses. According to Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc., what should the court do with the petition?

choices.A: Extend the injunction until the patent owner's damages claim is resolved.
choices.B: Remand the case to the intellectual property office for a fresh hearing.
choices.C: Convert the petition into an action for damages.
choices.D: Dismiss it, because with the patent no longer valid, the question of extending the injunction is moot and academic.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The Court said that the Court of Appeals should have granted the motion to dismiss the petition for certiorari, since the only issue raised was the propriety of extending the writ of preliminary injunction issued by the BLA-IPO. Because the patent that was the basis of the injunction was no longer valid, any issue about extending the life of the injunction was already rendered moot and academic. A is wrong because once the patent had lapsed, there was no right left to protect. B and C are not what the Court ordered; it dismissed the petition for certiorari for being moot and academic.

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the first issue (mootness of the extension of the injunction)
source.excerpt: In fact, the CA should have granted petitioner's motion to dismiss the petition for certiorari filed before it as the only issue raised therein is the propriety of extending the writ of preliminary injunction issued by the BLA-IPO. Since the patent which was the basis for issuing the injunction, was no longer valid, any issue as to the propriety of extending the life of the injunction was already rendered moot and academic.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A party files two actions that amount to forum shopping, but the forum shopping is not willful and deliberate, and the party told the second court about the pending first case. According to Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc., what is the consequence?

choices.A: Both cases are dismissed with prejudice.
choices.B: The subsequent case is dismissed without prejudice, on the ground of litis pendentia or res judicata.
choices.C: The first case is dismissed, and the subsequent case continues.
choices.D: Neither case is dismissed, and the party only pays a fine.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Court said that if forum shopping is not willful and deliberate, the subsequent case is dismissed without prejudice on the ground of either litis pendentia or res judicata, while if it is willful and deliberate, both (or all) actions are dismissed with prejudice. It found that Pfizer did not deliberately violate the rule, because it could erroneously believe that it could file separate actions on the basis of different patents, and because it candidly told the trial court of the pending complaint and petition. So only the Makati civil case was dismissed, on the ground of litis pendentia. A describes the consequence of willful and deliberate forum shopping. C and D are not what the Court held.

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the third issue (consequence of forum shopping)
source.excerpt: Jurisprudence holds that if the forum shopping is not considered willful and deliberate, the subsequent case shall be dismissed without prejudice, on the ground of either litis pendentia or res judicata. However, if the forum shopping is willful and deliberate, both (or all, if there are more than two) actions shall be dismissed with prejudice. In the present case, the Court finds that respondents did not deliberately violate the rule on non-forum shopping. Respondents may not be totally blamed for erroneously believing that they can file separate actions simply on the basis of different patents. Moreover, in the suit filed with the RTC of Makati City, respondents were candid enough to inform the trial court of the pendency of the complaint filed with the BLA-IPO as well as the petition for certiorari filed with the CA. On these bases, only Civil Case No. 04-754 should be dismissed on the ground of litis pendentia.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A patent owner files its infringement complaint with the intellectual property office instead of a regular court. The defendant argues that this was wrong. According to Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc., why was filing the complaint with the intellectual property office first proper?

choices.A: Because the doctrine of primary jurisdiction applies: deciding whether the defendant violated the patent rights requires the agency's sound administrative discretion, based on its special competence, knowledge and experience.
choices.B: Because regular courts have no jurisdiction over patent matters of any kind.
choices.C: Because the defendant had agreed in advance to file there.
choices.D: Because the agency's decisions are never subject to review by any court.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Court said that in specialized disputes the practice is to refer them to an administrative agency of special competence under the doctrine of primary jurisdiction, and it found that the initial filing with the BLA-IPO was in keeping with that doctrine because determining whether the petitioner violated the respondents' patent rights requires the exercise by the IPO of sound administrative discretion based on the agency's special competence, knowledge and experience. B is wrong because the doctrine applies where the claim is originally cognizable in the courts but its enforcement requires resolving issues placed within the special competence of an administrative body, in which case the court suspends its process and refers those issues to the agency. C has no basis in the decision. D is wrong because the Court itself reviewed the matter, and the Court of Appeals could review the interlocutory order by certiorari.

source.caseTitle: Philippine Pharmawealth, Inc. v. Pfizer, Inc. and Pfizer (Phil.) Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the second issue (the doctrine of primary jurisdiction)
source.excerpt: Based on the foregoing, the Court finds that respondents' initial filing of their complaint with the BLA-IPO, instead of the regular courts, is in keeping with the doctrine of primary jurisdiction owing to the fact that the determination of the basic issue of whether petitioner violated respondents' patent rights requires the exercise by the IPO of sound administrative discretion which is based on the agency's special competence, knowledge and experience.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A small company has sold a bottled drink under the name COOLY since 2022 but never registered the name. In 2024, a rival that had never heard of COOLY files an application for a confusingly similar name, COOLIE, for the same kind of drink, and the mark is registered. Who owns the right to the registered mark, and does it matter that the small company used its name first? Explain, based on Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The rival owns the mark it registered. Under the Intellectual Property Code, ownership of a mark is acquired through valid registration, not through prior use, so the small company's earlier use does not make it the owner.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Section 122 of the Intellectual Property Code provides that the rights in a mark are acquired through registration made validly in accordance with the Code. Section 123.1(d), the first-to-file rule, bars the registration of a mark identical or confusingly similar to a registered mark of a different proprietor or to a mark with an earlier filing or priority date. The Code removed the phrase "previously used in the Philippines by another and not abandoned" that the Trademark Law had in the corresponding provision, which shows that the lawmakers abandoned the rule that ownership is acquired by use. Actual use is still required, but only to maintain the registration and the registered owner's ownership, not as a way of acquiring ownership. For marks first used or registered after the Code took effect, ownership no longer depends on prior use.
suggestedAnswer.application: Both COOLY and COOLIE were used or registered after the Code took effect, so the use-based rule of the old Trademark Law does not apply. The rival registered in good faith, with no knowledge of COOLY, and registration gave it ownership. The small company, as an unregistered prior user, does not own COOLY as against the rival and cannot ask for cancellation of the registration merely because it used the name first.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The rival is the owner of the registered mark. The small company's prior use does not give it ownership, though, as the Court recognized in the same case, a prior user in good faith has other protection (Section 159.1).

keyPoints: Section 122: rights in a mark are acquired through registration made validly under the Code
Section 123.1(d), the first-to-file rule, bars the registration of confusingly similar marks of later applicants
The Code dropped the phrase "previously used in the Philippines by another and not abandoned": prior use no longer determines ownership
Actual use under the Code is needed to maintain ownership, not to acquire it
Use-based rulings under the old Trademark Law do not apply to marks used or registered after the Code took effect

source.caseTitle: Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc.
source.part: Part I (how trademark ownership is acquired)
source.excerpt: SECTION 122. How Marks are Acquired. - The rights in a mark shall be acquired through registration made validly in accordance with the provisions of this law. (Sec. 2-A, R.A. No. 166a) … Once the IP Code took effect, however, the general rule on ownership was changed and repealed. At present, as expressed in the language of the provisions of the IP Code, prior use no longer determines the acquisition of ownership of a mark in light of the adoption of the rule that ownership of a mark is acquired through registration made validly in accordance with the provisions of the IP Code. … To emphasize, for marks that are first used and/or registered after the effectivity of the IP Code, ownership is no longer dependent on the fact of prior use in light of the adoption of the first-to-file rule and the rule that ownership is acquired through registration.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A prior user of an unregistered brand claims that the company that later registered a confusingly similar brand did so in bad faith, because both companies advertise in the same industry directory and exhibited at the same trade conventions before the registration. The registrant says that it coined its brand from a medical term and checked the industry index and the government databases for similar names, and found none. Was the registration made in bad faith? Explain, based on Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Bad faith means knowledge of another's prior creation, use or registration of the mark. The prior user showed only a possibility of knowledge, which is not enough, and good faith is presumed.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Bad faith in a trademark registration means that the applicant or registrant has knowledge of prior creation, use and/or registration by another of an identical or similar trademark, in other words, copying and using somebody else's trademark. The presence of bad faith alone renders a trademark registration void. As a rule, good faith is always presumed, and the burden of proving bad faith rests on the one who alleges it.
suggestedAnswer.application: The prior user's evidence tended to show only that someone at the registrant might have known of its brand because they attended the same conferences and advertised in the same directory. A possibility is not sufficient to prove bad faith, especially when weighed against the registrant's explanation of how it coined its brand and the steps it took to make sure that no confusingly similar mark existed: it checked the industry index and the government databases. The prior user, who alleged bad faith, failed to carry its burden.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The registration was not made in bad faith, so it remains valid and the registrant acquired the rights of a trademark owner.

keyPoints: Bad faith = knowledge by the applicant or registrant of prior creation, use and/or registration by another of an identical or similar mark
A registration obtained in bad faith is void
Good faith is presumed, and the one alleging bad faith has the burden of proof
A mere possibility that the registrant knew, such as attending the same conferences or advertising in the same directory, is not enough
The registrant's checking of databases and its explanation of how it coined the name supported good faith

source.caseTitle: Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc.
source.part: Part II (bad faith and good faith in trademark registration) and Part III (the resolution of the controversy)
source.excerpt: Bad faith means that the applicant or registrant has knowledge of prior creation, use and/or registration by another of an identical or similar trademark. … To emphasize, the presence of bad faith alone renders void the trademark registrations. … As a rule, good faith is always presumed, and upon him who alleges bad faith on the part of a possessor rests the burden of proof. … Zuneca's evidence only tends to prove that there was a possibility that someone from Natrapharm might have known of Zuneca's use of "ZYNAPS" because Natrapharm and Zuneca attended the same conferences and that Zuneca had listed "ZYNAPS" in the PPD publication. Such possibility is not, however, sufficient to prove bad faith, especially when weighed against Natrapharm's evidence and explanation on how it coined "ZYNAPSE" and the steps it took to ensure that there were no other marks that were confusingly similar to it.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company registers a mark. A smaller business that has used a confusingly similar mark in good faith since before the registration, and never registered it, continues to use it. The registrant sues the smaller business for trademark infringement, arguing that the exception for prior users covers only use before the registration. Will the infringement suit prosper, and may the court order damages, an injunction or destruction of the smaller business's goods? Explain, based on Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. A prior user in good faith may continue to use its mark even after the registration, so it is not liable for infringement, and because there is no infringement the court cannot order damages, an injunction or destruction of goods.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Section 159.1 of the Intellectual Property Code provides that, notwithstanding Section 155, a registered mark has no effect against any person who, in good faith, before the filing date or the priority date, was using the mark for the purposes of his business or enterprise, and that his right may be transferred or assigned only together with his enterprise or business or the part in which the mark is used. Section 159.1 is an exception to the rights of the trademark owner under Section 147.1. The remedies in Sections 156 and 157 (damages, injunction, and disposal or destruction of infringing goods) may be ordered only if there is a finding of infringement.
suggestedAnswer.application: Reading Section 159.1 as exempting only use before the registration would make the provision useless, because even without it a third party's use of a then-unregistered mark could not be infringement, and it would make its proviso on transfer of the mark absurd. Read as a whole, it allows the prior user in good faith to continue using its mark after the registrant's registration, tied to its current business. So the smaller business is not liable for infringement. Since the remedies depend on a finding of infringement, no damages, injunction or destruction of goods can be ordered. The result is that two parties may use identical or confusingly similar marks at the same time, which may not be ideal but is what the provision says.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The infringement suit fails, and the lower courts' penalties could not stand. The smaller business may continue to use its mark with its business.

keyPoints: Section 159.1: a registered mark has no effect against a person who, in good faith, before the filing or priority date, was using the mark in his business
The prior user in good faith may continue using the mark even after registration, and may transfer it only together with its business
Reading Section 159.1 as covering only use before registration would make it useless and would make its proviso absurd
Section 159.1 is an exception to the owner's rights under Section 147.1
Damages, injunction and destruction of goods (Sections 156 and 157) may be ordered only upon a finding of infringement

source.caseTitle: Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc.
source.part: Part III (the resolution of the controversy, Section 159.1)
source.excerpt: Read as a whole, Section 159.1 of the IP Code clearly contemplates that a prior user in good faith may continue to use its mark even after the registration of the mark by the first-to-file registrant in good faith, subject to the condition that any transfer or assignment of the mark by the prior user in good faith should be made together with the enterprise or business or with that part of his enterprise or business in which the mark is used. The mark cannot be transferred independently of the enterprise and business using it. … A plain reading of the above provisions reveals that that these remedies may only be ordered by the court if there was a finding that a party had committed infringement. Here, because of the application of Section 159.1 of the IP Code, Zuneca is not liable for trademark infringement. Consequently, it follows that the award of damages, issuance of an injunction, and the disposition and/or destruction of allegedly infringing goods could not be ordered by the court. … Essentially, therefore, Section 159.1 is an exception to the rights of the trademark owner in Section 147.1 of the IP Code.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: According to Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc., which of the following must be proven to establish trademark infringement?

choices.A: That the infringer sells goods of lower quality than the trademark owner's goods.
choices.B: That the infringer first used the mark before the trademark owner did.
choices.C: That the trademark owner has used the mark for at least ten years.
choices.D: That the trademark being infringed is registered in the IPO and the infringer's use is likely to cause confusion or mistake, or to deceive, without the trademark owner's consent.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The Court listed the elements of trademark infringement: (1) the trademark being infringed is registered in the IPO; (2) the trademark is reproduced, counterfeited, copied or colorably imitated by the infringer; (3) the infringing mark is used in connection with the sale, offering for sale or advertising of goods, business or services, or is applied to labels, signs, packages or advertisements for them; (4) the use is likely to cause confusion or mistake or to deceive purchasers or others as to the goods or services or their source; and (5) it is without the consent of the trademark owner or the assignee. A is wrong because the quality of the infringer's goods is not an element. B is wrong because prior use by the infringer is not an element and does not make a registered mark's owner lose; under the Code, ownership comes from registration. C is wrong because the Code does not require ten years of use.

source.caseTitle: Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc.
source.part: The Court's Ruling (the elements of trademark infringement)
source.excerpt: Further, in Prosource International, Inc. v. Horphag Research Management SA, the Court held that, to establish trademark infringement, the following elements must be proven: … the trademark being infringed is registered in the IPO; (2) the trademark is reproduced, counterfeited, copied, or colorably imitated by the infringer; (3) the infringing mark is used in connection with the sale, offering for sale, or advertising of any goods, business, or services; or the infringing mark is applied to labels, signs, prints, packages, wrappers, receptacles, or advertisements intended to be used upon or in connection with such goods, business, or services; (4) the use or application of the infringing mark is likely to cause confusion or mistake or to deceive purchasers or others as to the goods or services themselves or as to the source or origin of such goods or services or the identity of such business; and (5) it is without the consent of the trademark owner or the assignee thereof.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In an earlier case, Berris Agricultural Co., Inc. v. Abyadang, the Court said that "the ownership of a trademark is acquired by its registration and its actual use." What did Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc. do with that statement?

choices.A: It reaffirmed the statement as the current rule on acquiring ownership.
choices.B: It rectified the statement: under the IP Code, ownership of a trademark is acquired by its registration.
choices.C: It reversed the result in Berris and declared the prior user the owner.
choices.D: It held that the statement applies only to foreign trademarks.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Court said that after the IP Code became effective in 1998, use was no longer required to acquire or perfect ownership of a mark, and it rectified the inaccurate statement in Berris. The rectified statement reads: "Under the IP Code, the ownership of a trademark is acquired by its registration." The result in Berris was still right because the winner was the first to file and register. The Court added that proof of subsequent use is required to prevent the removal or cancellation of a registered mark or the refusal of a pending application, but this does not mean that actual use is necessary before one can own the mark or exercise the rights of an owner. A is wrong because the Court corrected the statement. C is wrong because Berris was correct in its result, based on first filing and registration. D is wrong because the Court did not limit the statement to foreign marks.

source.caseTitle: Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc.
source.part: Part I (the rule in Berris)
source.excerpt: To repeat, after the IP Code became effective starting 1998, use was no longer required in order to acquire or perfect ownership of the mark. In this regard, the Court now rectifies the inaccurate statement in Berris that "[t]he ownership of a trademark is acquired by its registration and its actual use." The rectified statement should thus read: "Under the IP Code, the ownership of a trademark is acquired by its registration."

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: The Intellectual Property Code requires a registrant to file a declaration of actual use of the mark and to prove continued use. A prior user argues that this shows that actual use is still a way to acquire ownership of a mark. According to Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc., how should these provisions be understood?

choices.A: As provisions requiring actual use so that the registered owner can maintain his ownership; they do not make actual use a mode of acquiring ownership.
choices.B: As proof that the Code still follows the old Trademark Law rule that use creates ownership.
choices.C: As provisions that apply only to unregistered marks.
choices.D: As optional rules that the registrant may ignore.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Court said that while the Code and the IPO rules require the applicant or registrant to prove continued actual use, this does not imply that actual use is still a recognized mode of acquiring ownership. Rather, these provisions require actual use of the mark so that the registered owner can maintain his ownership. The Court answered the similar argument about the prima facie effect of the certificate of registration in the same way: it shows when a certificate does not reflect ownership, for example when the first registrant lost ownership through non-use or abandonment, or the registration was done in bad faith or contrary to the Code. B is wrong because the Court held that the old use-based regime was abandoned. C is wrong because the requirement applies to registrants and applicants. D is wrong because failure to file the declaration of actual use can cause the mark to be removed or the application to be refused.

source.caseTitle: Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc.
source.part: Part I (continued actual use under the IP Code)
source.excerpt: Certainly, while the IP Code and the Rules of the IPO mandate that the applicant/registrant must prove continued actual use of the mark, it is the considered view of the Court that this does not imply that actual use is still a recognized mode of acquisition of ownership under the IP Code. Rather, these must be understood as provisions that require actual use of the mark in order for the registered owner of a mark to maintain his ownership.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: According to Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc., what does the removal of the phrase "previously used in the Philippines by another and not abandoned" from the provision on unregistrable marks (the old Section 4(d) of the Trademark Law, now Section 123.1(d) of the IP Code) show?

choices.A: That unregistered marks can no longer be used in the Philippines at all.
choices.B: That only foreign marks may be registered.
choices.C: That a good faith applicant may register a mark that was previously used and not abandoned by another, and the prior user can no longer ask for cancellation on that ground; it shows the lawmakers' intent to abandon the use-based regime.
choices.D: That every registration is conclusive and can never be cancelled.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Court explained that under the Trademark Law the first user could file a cancellation case against an identical or confusingly similar mark registered in good faith by another, but with the phrase omitted in the IP Code, that right is no longer available. A good faith applicant may still register a mark previously used and not abandoned by another and become its owner, and the prior user cannot ask for cancellation of the registration. If the lawmakers had wanted to retain ownership through use, they would have kept the phrase to avoid conflicts in ownership. A is wrong because the unregistered prior user in good faith may continue to use its mark under Section 159.1. B has nothing to do with the phrase. D is wrong because the Court recognized other grounds for cancellation, such as registration obtained in bad faith or contrary to the Code.

source.caseTitle: Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc.
source.part: Part I (the language of Sections 122 and 123.1(d))
source.excerpt: Subparagraph (d) of the above provision of the Trademark Law was amended in the IP Code to, among others, remove the phrase "previously used in the Philippines by another and not abandoned." … In effect, based on the language of the provisions of the IP Code, even if the mark was previously used and not abandoned by another person, a good faith applicant may still register the same and thus become the owner thereof, and the prior user cannot ask for the cancellation of the latter's registration.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: The two medicines in Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc. had admittedly confusingly similar brand names but treated different diseases, and the Court did not stop either party from using its mark. What did the Court order to reduce the likelihood of medical switching?

choices.A: That one of the two companies change its brand name within six months.
choices.B: That both drugs be sold only in pharmacies of the registrant.
choices.C: That the Food and Drug Administration cancel the registration of both drugs.
choices.D: That each company state on its packaging, in plain language, the conditions its drug is supposed to treat and a warning about what the drug is not supposed to treat, with the Food and Drug Administration to monitor compliance.

questions.explanation: D is correct. The Court ordered the parties to prominently state on their packaging, in plain language understandable by people with no medical background, the medical conditions their drugs are supposed to treat or alleviate and a warning indicating what "ZYNAPS" is not supposed to treat and what "ZYNAPSE" is not supposed to treat. The parties must submit a written report of compliance within thirty days, and the Court furnished the Food and Drug Administration a copy and directed it to monitor compliance. The Court noted that the Generics Act requires doctors to write prescriptions using the generic name, so the evil of medical switching will likely not arise, but it was still mindful of the risk to public health. A, B and C are not orders in the decision; the Court actually allowed both marks to coexist because the prior user in good faith is protected by Section 159.1.

source.caseTitle: Zuneca Pharmaceutical v. Natrapharm, Inc.
source.part: Part III (the resolution of the controversy, medical switching)
source.excerpt: To further reduce therefore, if not totally eliminate, the likelihood of switching in this case, the Court hereby orders the parties to prominently state on the packaging of their respective products, in plain language understandable by people with no medical background or training, the medical conditions that their respective drugs are supposed to treat or alleviate and a warning indicating what "ZYNAPS" is not supposed to treat and what "ZYNAPSE" is not supposed to treat, given the likelihood of confusion between the two.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A company owns the registered mark GLOWRIN for skin creams. A beauty clinic applies to register GLOWRINE, written in a fancy script with a flower design, for facial treatment services. The clinic argues that its mark looks completely different when its whole design is compared with the plain GLOWRIN, and that services and creams are in different classes. Should the application be rejected? Explain, based on Dermaline, Inc. v. Myra Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. The two marks are confusingly similar under the Dominancy Test. A different presentation and a different classification do not remove the likelihood of confusion, especially since both concern skin care.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: A registered trademark owner may prevent others from using an identical or similar mark where such use would result in a likelihood of confusion (Section 147). Likelihood of confusion is determined by the Dominancy Test, which focuses on the similarity of the prevalent features of the marks and which asks whether the ordinary purchaser would likely be confused, giving greater weight to the aural and visual impressions created by the marks and little weight to factors like price, quality, sales outlets and market segments. It is written into Section 155.1. The Holistic Test, which looks at the entirety of the marks, is the alternative. Classification of goods or services does not eradicate the possibility of mistake in associating one mark with the other.
suggestedAnswer.application: GLOWRINE is spelled almost the same as GLOWRIN, differing only by a final letter that is silent, and the two are pronounced in practically the same way. The fancy script and flower design only differ in presentation, and an ordinary buyer who hears the clinic advertised on the radio would likely associate it with the registered brand. The different classes do not help, because both the creams and the treatments concern the skin, and the public may think that the cream maker has expanded its business into skin services. Such an expansion is the normal potential expansion of its business, which the registered owner is entitled to protect.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The application should be rejected, because the marks are confusingly similar and the registered owner's rights are protected.

keyPoints: The registered owner may prevent the use of identical or similar marks that would likely cause confusion (Section 147)
Dominancy Test: similarity of the prevalent features; greater weight to the aural and visual impressions on the ordinary purchaser; written into Section 155.1
Holistic Test: the entirety of the marks, including labels and packaging
Almost identical spelling and practically identical pronunciation point to likely confusion
A different classification does not eradicate the possibility of mistake, especially where both concern the same kind of treatment
The registered owner is protected in the normal potential expansion of its business

source.caseTitle: Dermaline, Inc. v. Myra Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the dominancy test and the comparison of the marks
source.excerpt: In determining likelihood of confusion, case law has developed two (2) tests, the Dominancy Test and the Holistic or Totality Test. The Dominancy Test focuses on the similarity of the prevalent features of the competing trademarks that might cause confusion or deception. … Given greater consideration are the aural and visual impressions created by the marks in the public mind, giving little weight to factors like prices, quality, sales outlets, and market segments. … While it is true that the two marks are presented differently … the likelihood of confusion is still apparent. This is because they are almost spelled in the same way, except for Dermaline’s mark which ends with the letter "E," and they are pronounced practically in the same manner in three (3) syllables, with the ending letter "E" in Dermaline’s mark pronounced silently. Thus, when an ordinary purchaser, for example, hears an advertisement of Dermaline’s applied trademark over the radio, chances are he will associate it with Myra’s registered mark.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A trademark owner makes medicated creams under a registered mark. A new company seeks to register a nearly identical mark for health and beauty services, which belong to a different class. It argues that no one could think that a cream maker also runs beauty salons. Is the argument correct? Explain the two kinds of confusion in trademark cases and the scope of the registered owner's protection, based on Dermaline, Inc. v. Myra Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. A trademark owner's protection is not limited to identical goods in actual competition. It extends to cases where buyers would be misled into thinking that the owner has expanded its business or is connected with the other party, which is the normal potential expansion of its business.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Jurisprudence recognizes two types of confusion: (1) confusion of goods (product confusion), where the ordinarily prudent purchaser would buy one product thinking that it was the other; and (2) confusion of business (source or origin confusion), where the goods of the parties are different but the product is such as might reasonably be assumed to originate with the registrant of an earlier product, or the public would be deceived into believing that there is some connection between the two parties, though none exists. The registered owner may use its mark on the same or similar products, in different segments of the market and at different price levels, and it enjoys protection in the product and market areas that are the normal potential expansion of its business. Protection extends to all cases in which use by a junior appropriator is likely to lead to a confusion of source, as where buyers would be misled into thinking that the complaining party has extended its business into the field or is in any way connected with the infringer's activities.
suggestedAnswer.application: Even if the services are in a different class from the creams, the public may mistakenly think that the new company is connected with the cream maker, especially with the current proliferation of health and beauty products in the market. They may believe that the owner has already expanded from medicated skin products to health and beauty services. That is confusion of business, and the expansion is a normal potential one, so the argument that no one would link the two businesses fails. The difference in classification does not eradicate the possibility of mistake.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The argument is not correct. The registered owner is protected against confusion of business, and the application should not be allowed.

keyPoints: Two types of confusion: confusion of goods (product confusion) and confusion of business (source or origin confusion)
Confusion of business can exist even if the goods of the parties are different
The registered owner's protection is not limited to actual competition with identical or similar products
It extends to the normal potential expansion of its business
A different classification of goods or services does not remove the possibility of mistake

source.caseTitle: Dermaline, Inc. v. Myra Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the types of confusion and the owner's protection
source.excerpt: Relative to the question on confusion of marks and trade names, jurisprudence has noted two (2) types of confusion, viz: (1) confusion of goods (product confusion), where the ordinarily prudent purchaser would be induced to purchase one product in the belief that he was purchasing the other; and (2) confusion of business (source or origin confusion), where, although the goods of the parties are different, the product, the mark of which registration is applied for by one party, is such as might reasonably be assumed to originate with the registrant of an earlier product, and the public would then be deceived either into that belief or into the belief that there is some connection between the two parties, though inexistent. … The Court is cognizant that the registered trademark owner enjoys protection in product and market areas that are the normal potential expansion of his business. … Thus, the public may mistakenly think that Dermaline is connected to or associated with Myra, such that, considering the current proliferation of health and beauty products in the market, the purchasers would likely be misled that Myra has already expanded its business through Dermaline from merely carrying pharmaceutical topical applications for the skin to health and beauty services.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: An applicant seeks to register a mark that closely resembles an already registered mark. The owner of the registered mark does not file any opposition. Must the application nevertheless be rejected? Also, on appeal, the applicant asks the Supreme Court to re-evaluate the facts about whether the marks are confusingly similar. How should the Court treat the findings of the intellectual property office? Explain, based on Dermaline, Inc. v. Myra Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes to the first, and the findings are respected on the second. An application for a mark that is almost the same as or closely resembles a mark already used and registered should be rejected outright, even without opposition, and the intellectual property office's factual findings, upheld by the Court of Appeals, carry great weight.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: When one applies for the registration of a trademark or label that is almost the same as or that very closely resembles one already used and registered by another, the application should be rejected and dismissed outright, even without any opposition on the part of the owner and user of the previously registered mark. This is intended not only to avoid confusion on the part of the public but also to protect an already used and registered trademark and an established goodwill. The protection of intellectual property such as trademarks is a factual issue, so the findings of the IPO, upheld on appeal by the same office and sustained by the Court of Appeals, bear great weight and deserve respect from the Court.
suggestedAnswer.application: Because the applied mark closely resembles the registered one, the office could properly reject it even if the owner had not opposed. On review, the applicant's argument that the marks are different is a factual challenge, and the office, whose findings were upheld by the Court of Appeals, found likelihood of confusion. The Court gives those findings great weight and respect. In the case itself, the IPO decision had also become final because the applicant did not appeal to the Director General on time.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The application must be rejected even without an opposition, and the Court will defer to the office's affirmed factual findings of confusing similarity.

The purpose is to avoid confusion of the public and to protect a registered mark and its established goodwill
The protection of trademarks is a factual issue
The IPO's findings, upheld by the Court of Appeals, bear great weight and deserve respect
A decision of the IPO becomes final if the appeal to the Director General is not filed on time

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: In Dermaline, Inc. v. Myra Pharmaceuticals, Inc., the Court described the Dominancy Test. Which statement correctly describes it?

choices.A: It requires that the applied mark be an exact duplicate of the registered mark.
choices.B: It focuses on the similarity of the prevalent features of the competing marks, and it is applied when the applied mark contains the main, essential and dominant features of the earlier mark and confusion is likely to result.
choices.C: It looks mainly at prices, quality and sales outlets to decide whether buyers would be confused.
choices.D: It compares the whole labels and packaging of the two products, and gives no weight to the sound of the marks.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Dominancy Test focuses on the similarity of the prevalent features of the competing trademarks that might cause confusion or deception, and it applies when the mark sought to be registered contains the main, essential and dominant features of the earlier registered mark and confusion is likely. Duplication or imitation is not even required. The important issue is whether use of the marks would likely cause confusion or mistake in the mind of the ordinary purchaser, with greater consideration given to the aural and visual impressions the marks create. A is wrong because duplication or imitation is not required. C is wrong because the test gives little weight to prices, quality, sales outlets and market segments. D describes the Holistic Test, which looks at the entirety of the marks including labels and packaging.

source.caseTitle: Dermaline, Inc. v. Myra Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
source.part: Discussion of the dominancy test
source.excerpt: The Dominancy Test focuses on the similarity of the prevalent features of the competing trademarks that might cause confusion or deception. It is applied when the trademark sought to be registered contains the main, essential and dominant features of the earlier registered trademark, and confusion or deception is likely to result. questions.prompt: According to Dermaline, Inc. v. Myra Pharmaceuticals, Inc., which provision of the Intellectual Property Code explicitly incorporates the dominancy test into law?

choices.A: Section 122, on how marks are acquired.
choices.B: Section 138, on the certificate of registration as prima facie evidence.
choices.C: Section 155.1, which prohibits the use in commerce of any reproduction, counterfeit, copy or colorable imitation of a registered mark or the same container or a dominant feature thereof, where such use is likely to cause confusion, mistake or deception.
choices.D: Section 147, on the rights conferred by registration.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Court said that the test of dominancy is now explicitly incorporated into law in Section 155.1, which covers use in commerce of any reproduction, counterfeit, copy or colorable imitation of a registered mark or the same container or a dominant feature thereof in connection with the sale, offering for sale, distribution or advertising of goods or services, where such use is likely to cause confusion, or to cause mistake, or to deceive. The reference to a dominant feature is what writes the dominancy test into law. A, B and D are real provisions that the decision mentions for other purposes: Section 147 gives the registered owner the right to prevent others from using identical or similar marks that would likely cause confusion, and Section 138 makes the certificate of registration prima facie evidence of validity, ownership and exclusive right to use; neither is the provision that incorporates the dominancy test.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A famous foreign restaurant chain has never registered its name in the Philippines and has never operated here, although the name is well known internationally and among Filipinos. A local company applies to register the same name for restaurants and argues that, because the chain has not used or registered the mark in the Philippines, the chain has no rights here and the local company, as first to file, should win. Is the local company right? Explain, based on Fredco Manufacturing Corp. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. An internationally well-known mark is protected in the Philippines even if it is neither registered nor used here. The territoriality principle, which requires use in the Philippines, has an exception for such marks.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The Philippines is a party to the Paris Convention and is obliged to assure nationals of other member countries effective protection against violations of their intellectual property rights here. Article 6bis requires the refusal or cancellation of the registration, and the prohibition of the use, of a mark that is a reproduction or imitation of a mark considered by the competent authority to be already the mark of a person entitled to the Convention's benefits and used for identical or similar goods. Under the directives of the Ministry of Trade, an internationally well-known mark need not be registered or used in the Philippines; it is enough that the mark is well-known internationally and in the Philippines for identical or similar goods. Section 123.1(e) of the Intellectual Property Code likewise bars the registration of a mark considered by the competent authority to be well-known internationally and in the Philippines, whether or not it is registered here. Under Rule 102 of the implementing rules, a mark is shown to be well-known by any combination of criteria, such as the duration and geographical area of its use and promotion, the extent to which it has been registered and used in the world, and its reputation and commercial value, so use in the Philippines is not necessary.
suggestedAnswer.application: The chain's name is well known internationally and among Filipinos, as shown by criteria such as worldwide use, registration and reputation. The mark was therefore already protected in the Philippines even before the chain applied here, as the Court found for the Harvard mark. The local company, which copied the name, cannot rely on being first to file and on the chain's lack of use or registration in the Philippines.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The local company is wrong. The famous chain's mark is protected, and the local application should not be allowed.

keyPoints: The Philippines must assure nationals of Paris Convention countries effective protection of their intellectual property rights
Article 6bis of the Paris Convention protects well-known marks
An internationally well-known mark need not be registered or used in the Philippines; it must be well-known internationally and in the Philippines for identical or similar goods
Section 123.1(e) of the IP Code bars registration of a mark considered well-known internationally and in the Philippines, whether or not registered here
Rule 102 criteria (any combination) show that a mark is well-known; use in the Philippines is not required
Exception to the territoriality principle

source.caseTitle: Fredco Manufacturing Corp. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College (Harvard University)
source.part: The Ruling of this Court (the second reason: the Paris Convention and well-known marks)
source.excerpt: Thus, this Court has ruled that the Philippines is obligated to assure nationals of countries of the Paris Convention that they are afforded an effective protection against violation of their intellectual property rights in the Philippines in the same way that their own countries are obligated to accord similar protection to Philippine nationals. … To be protected under the two directives of the Ministry of Trade, an internationally well-known mark need not be registered or used in the Philippines. All that is required is that the mark is well-known internationally and in the Philippines for identical or similar goods, whether or not the mark is registered or used in the Philippines. … Rule 102. Criteria for determining whether a mark is well-known. In determining whether a mark is well-known, the following criteria or any combination thereof may be taken into account: … (e) the extent to which the mark has been registered in the world; … As such, even before Harvard University applied for registration of the mark "Harvard" in the Philippines, the mark was already protected under Article 6bis and Article 8 of the Paris Convention.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A local clothing company registers the name of a famous foreign university as its brand. Its logo also carries the words "Established 1936", "USA" and the university's city, although the company has no connection with the university, the city or the United States. The company later says that it used these words only "to evoke a lifestyle". May the registration stand? Explain, based on Fredco Manufacturing Corp. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The registration should not have been allowed, because the mark falsely suggests a connection with the university. Section 4(a) of the Trademark Law prohibits the registration of such a mark, and the violation is a ground for cancellation.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Section 4(a) of R.A. No. 166 prohibits the registration of a mark that consists of or comprises matter that may disparage or falsely suggest a connection with persons, living or dead, institutions, beliefs or national symbols. The provision is identical to Section 2(a) of the Lanham Act of the United States and is intended to protect the right of publicity of famous individuals and institutions from the commercial exploitation of their goodwill by others. Under Section 17(c) of R.A. No. 166, a registration obtained in violation of Section 4 may be cancelled.
suggestedAnswer.application: The company has no affiliation with the university or its city, and it was not established in 1936 or in the United States, yet its logo combines the university's name with these words. That obviously suggests a false connection with the university. The company's belated explanation that it wished to evoke a lifestyle or a desirable aura only confirms that it sought to connect its products with the university and to ride on its prestige and popularity, appropriating part of its goodwill without its consent. That is exactly the commercial exploitation of goodwill that Section 4(a) forbids.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The registration should have been disallowed, and the violation of Section 4(a) is a ground for cancelling it under Section 17(c).

keyPoints: Section 4(a) of R.A. No. 166 prohibits registering a mark that may falsely suggest a connection with persons, institutions, beliefs or national symbols
Use of the famous name together with a claimed origin in the university's city and "Established 1936" and "USA" suggests a false connection
The provision protects the right of publicity of famous individuals and institutions against exploitation of their goodwill
A belated justification of evoking a desirable aura confirms the intent to connect the products with the university
Under Section 17(c), a registration obtained in violation of Section 4 is a ground for cancellation

No. 166 prohibits the registration of a mark "which may disparage or falsely suggest a connection with persons, living or dead, institutions, beliefs x x x." … Fredco’s use of the mark "Harvard," coupled with its claimed origin in Cambridge, Massachusetts, obviously suggests a false connection with Harvard University. On this ground alone, Fredco’s registration of the mark "Harvard" should have been disallowed. … Section 4(a) of R.A. No. 166 is identical to Section 2(a) of the Lanham Act, the trademark law of the United States. These provisions are intended to protect the right of publicity of famous individuals and institutions from commercial exploitation of their goodwill by others. … Under Section 17(c) of R.A. No. 166, such violation is a ground for cancellation of Fredco’s registration of the mark "Harvard" because the registration was obtained in violation of Section 4 of R.A. No. 166.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A foreign company registered its mark at home and then obtained a Philippine registration based on that home registration, without ever having used the mark in the Philippines. A local company that began using a similar mark in the Philippines earlier argues that its earlier actual use in the Philippines should prevail. Is the argument correct? Explain, based on Fredco Manufacturing Corp. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. A registration based on a home registration in a Paris Convention country does not require actual prior use of the mark in the Philippines, and any such defect was in any case cured by the Intellectual Property Code.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Section 2 of R.A. No. 166 requires, for the registration of a trademark, proof that it has actually been used in commerce in the Philippines for not less than two months before the application, but where the mark is already registered in a foreign country that is a member of the Paris Convention, that proof is not necessary, because Section 37 allows registration on the basis of a home registration. An applicant on a home registration need not even have used the mark in the country. Under Section 239.2 of R.A. No. 8293, marks registered under R.A. No. 166 remain in force but are deemed to have been granted under the new Code, which does not require actual prior use in the Philippines.
suggestedAnswer.application: The foreign company's registration rested on home registration, so its lack of prior use in the Philippines does not defeat it. Its registration is now deemed granted under the Intellectual Property Code, which does not require prior use here, so any defect arising from the absence of actual use in the Philippines has been cured. The local company's earlier use does not prevail. In the decision itself, the local claimant's own registration had been cancelled for failure to file the affidavit of use on the fifth anniversary, so it was no longer the registrant or presumptive owner.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The local company's argument fails, and the foreign company's registration is not defeated by the lack of actual use in the Philippines.

That proof is not necessary when the mark is registered in a foreign country that is a member of the Paris Convention (home registration, Section 37)
Under Section 239.2 of R.A. No. 8293, marks registered under R.A. No. 166 are deemed granted under the Code, which does not require actual prior use in the Philippines
Any defect from lack of prior use in the Philippines was cured by Section 239.2

This means that no educational entity in the Philippines can use the trade name "Harvard" without the consent of Harvard University.

questions.subject: Mercantile Law
questions.prompt: A local company relies on its own earlier registration of a mark to claim ownership against a foreign owner. But that registration had been cancelled years earlier because the company failed to file the required affidavit of use on the fifth anniversary of the registration. According to Fredco Manufacturing Corp. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, what is the effect on the company's position?

choices.A: The company remains the registrant and presumptive owner, because cancellation is only temporary.
choices.B: The company becomes the owner of every similar mark in the same class.
choices.C: At the time it brought its petition, the company was no longer the registrant or presumptive owner of the mark.
choices.D: The company's earlier registration is revived automatically when it brings a case.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Court noted that Fredco's registration was already cancelled on 30 July 1998 when it failed to file the required affidavit of use/non-use for the fifth anniversary of the registration. Hence, when Fredco filed its petition for cancellation before the Bureau of Legal Affairs, it was no longer the registrant or presumptive owner of the mark "Harvard". A and D are wrong because the decision treats the cancellation as removing that status. B has no basis in the decision.
